What can and can't do

Ahead of launch, Robocurve, a Public Benefit Corporation that measures and reports frontier robotics capabilities to the public, evaluated independently. Their report, above, shows is better, faster and cheaper: a new Pareto frontier for robot control. It scores above the next best models, Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, at 16x lower cost per task attempt than Gemini 4 Argon and 1.7x faster than the fastest LLM, GPT-6 Astra. While current LLMs excel at planning, robots still require a fast, general System 1 to act, and that is what is built to be.

How much does it cost to run ? We want you to know exactly what to expect before you try it. Running the model costs just $3 per hour for , or $2 per hour for Dream-1-flash. Each call to the model returns 1.6 seconds of actions, so an hour is 2,250 calls: about $0.0013 an action for , and $0.0009 for Dream-1-flash.

Everything above the hourly cost is yours to keep.

The faster, lighter model.

We break ’s performance down into eight task categories, from what it handles well to where it still struggles.

Fine-tune for your task with FaaS. If falls short on a task you care about, you don’t have to wait for our next release. Collect some data on your own robot, run it through FaaS, and get a custom model built for that task.

We want anyone with a robot to work like a forward-deployed engineer: find a task someone needs done, collect a bit of data, adapt to it, and deploy. If people will pay for what your robot does, you keep everything above the hourly cost.

items.title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.content:
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions.

“Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute.

Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected.

The work, published in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits was developed as part of a CHF 6.6 million grant from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on brain-to-text decoding and closed-loop neuromodulation, extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies.

More targeted stimulation at lower power

The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity.

Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system.

“Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding.

LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces.

In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through Infera Neuro, an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran.

items.title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads from Java Applications
items.author: pjmlp
items.content:
TornadoVM automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Rather than replacing existing JVMs, it works alongside them and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that you can use with any mainstream JDK distribution such as OpenJDK, Graalvm, Temurin, or Zulu.

It offloads Java code to hardware backends, manages memory between the Java heap and accelerators, and runs the resulting compute kernels. This makes it a useful building block for modern cloud and machine learning workloads.

During development, TornadoVM compiles the source Java code to OpenCL and Apple Metal backends. The idea is that you can develop locally on your laptop and use the hardware available locally, and then deploy into a server that has Nvidia GPUs, and achieve major performance improvements - a form of "Write Once, Run Anywhere" for modern ML workloads.

Version 7 brings several architectural changes. The backends now use the Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API in place of the Java Native Interface (JNI). The experimental JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI) dependency has also been removed. According to the team, TornadoVM now sources "all compiler metadata through a reflection + ASM + Unsafe layer" which is the single, uniform path on every supported JDK (21, 25, 26 and 27).

The release also deepens integration with the Nvidia ecosystem through an optimized CUDA backend. This includes support for the cuTile programming model (via a new ) and the ability to call CUDA libraries such as cuBLAS and CUTLASS directly from within TornadoVM TaskGraphs. Developers can swap JIT-generated kernels for CUDA library calls, or chain the two together, depending on their performance and portability needs. Similarly, TornadoVM adds the same functionality for Apple's MXL library again via the hybrid API. Finally, support for multi-GPU execution has been added.

Not every Java computation benefits from offloading. The best candidates are data-parallel workloads, such as loops with no dependencies between iterations, because their iterations can run in parallel on the accelerator.

One of the goals of recent TornadoVM versions is to produce an idiomatic JVM environment for accessing the libraries that Nvidia have been tuning for different hardware platforms. The aim is for Java developers to tap into things like Linear Algebra, Fast Fourier Transforms (for Signal Analysis), Deep Neural Networks and hand-optimized matrix multiplication for sparse matrices. TornadoVM has library integrations with Quarkus, Lang4j, Flink, Spring AI and others and is also available through SDKMan.

For example, consider the integration of Apache Flink with TornadoVM - the main idea is that the developer writes a standard query as they normally would with the Table API. A configuration flag is used to indicate that this query should potentially be accelerated on a GPU.

Then, when the computation reaches the task manager, the framework checks if there is a GPU available in the node it is executing on and, if so, it connects to a library provider - which analyzes the intermediate representation (IR) of the query to see if the computation is actually suitable for GPU execution.

In total, TornadoVM offers four ways to program Nvidia GPUs as a Java programmer - Firstly, the parallel API which is really just an annotation that annotates a loop, and provides a hint for the compiler that this loop can be potentially paralyzed. This simple API did not prove to be sufficient in the long-term to get the desired performance for production applications, so additional APIs were added - such as the kernel context API and the already-mentioned TileContext.

Alongside the 7.3 release, the TornadoVM team introduced jitLLM v2.0, its next-generation Java AI inference engine built on TornadoVM. The team positions jitLLM as a direct competitor to llama.cpp and Ollama in performance, and it ships as a single JAR file.

Both TornadoVM and jitLLM are being commercialized through Beestream.ai, a spin-off founded by the TornadoVM team.

items.title: Bringing uv and ty together
items.author: Ravencentric
items.content:
Experimental uv-ty integration is now available, enabling first-class support for Python scripts (on the CLI and in the editor) and a unified command.

This is a step towards an integrated Astral toolchain, one that uses a shared understanding of your project to enable entirely new capabilities.

At Astral, we build high-performance tools for the Python ecosystem: uv, our package manager; Ruff, our linter and formatter; and ty, our type checker and language server.

Historically, each Astral tool has focused on making a different component of Python development more productive. But we see an opportunity to further Python by unifying traditionally separate capabilities into an integrated toolchain.

Our vision for the Astral toolchain is simple: while each tool should be individually usable, useful, and interoperable with the rest of the ecosystem, they should be even more capable when used together.

Today, we’re announcing an experimental integration between uv and ty, available in preview. uv understands your Python project’s environment and dependencies, while ty understands your code. By combining the two, we can unlock new functionality beyond what either tool can provide individually.

First-class support for Python scripts#

PEP 723 enables Python scripts to declare their dependencies and Python version requirements through inline metadata. uv already uses this metadata to prepare an environment when running a script. Now, ty can use this metadata to understand your scripts.

On both the command line and in the editor, ty now uses inline metadata to discover scripts throughout your project and leverages uv to prepare an environment for each script. These environments allow ty to check your scripts against their declared requirements.

Scripts can have different requirements within the same repository. Each script is checked against its own dependency declarations, even if those dependencies or Python requirements differ from the surrounding project.

Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor.

Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor.

When the integration is enabled in your editor, ty automatically invokes uv to prepare the script’s environment in the background, which it uses to provide type checking, code navigation, and completions based on the script’s declared requirements.

Over time, we plan to enable script support by default, and enable automatic environment setup for standard Python projects.

A unified checking command#

introduces a unified diagnostic interface to uv, starting with support for ty. Over time, we plan to support Ruff in to unify linting and type checking into a single command.

Running will automatically prepare your project’s environment, install the required dependencies, and check your project with ty. It “just works.” (If you never run , nothing changes for your uv experience; the ty binary is installed separately on first invocation.)

With , you can check individual packages, or an entire workspace. In a workspace, use uv check --package <name> to select an individual package, or to check every package. uv uses your workspace configuration to determine what to check, so the command stays the same as your workspace grows.

Sync your project’s dependencies and type-check your code with a single command.

Sync your project’s dependencies and type-check your code with a single command.

Standalone PEP 723 scripts have independent environments and are checked separately. Use uv check --script example.py to check a script using its declared requirements.

automatically uses the ty version recorded in your project’s lockfile. Commit your project configuration and lockfile, and developers and CI running will share the same ty version without separately maintained pins.

The ty pre-commit hook also uses under the hood to run ty before each commit over your Python project. By using , the hook automatically sets up the environment for ty from your project’s dependency declarations.

The uv-ty integration is powered by , which gives ty a structured view of your project or script’s packages, dependencies, and Python environment. ty then uses this information to provide type checking and editor features that reflect the configured environment.

For PEP 723 scripts, ty invokes uv to prepare the script’s environment, which includes installing declared dependencies. As dependency installation can require execution of third-party Python code, automatic environment setup is currently opt-in.

You can also check your project and its PEP 723 scripts from the command line with:

Running enables the integration automatically and requires no additional configuration.

Support for PEP 723 scripts and the command requires uv 0.12.3 or later, and ty 0.0.76 or later.

This integration is experimental, and we’d love your feedback as we refine the experience.

While this initial support largely leverages uv’s environment capabilities to power ty execution, we’re also working on a new category of checks that combine uv’s knowledge of your project’s dependencies with ty’s understanding of your code (e.g., to detect unused dependencies), which we’ll cover in a future post.

And, in parallel, we’re continuing toward ty’s stable release.

Thank you for building with us!
